text:
When I moved my side project's database onto a 2 GB VPS, I assumed Postgres would cope just fine. It has a reputation for being sturdy, and my dataset was small. What I hadn't counted on was how fast memory runs out when you leave the defaults alone and let the application open as many connections as it wants.

I followed the usual advice and set shared_buffers to 512 MB, a quarter of the machine's RAM. That setting wasn't the problem. The problem was everything around it. The app could open up to 200 client connections, and each backend process uses memory of its own. That left the server with very little headroom, and the kernel noticed. In the first month, the OOM killer ran three times and took Postgres down every time.

The biggest improvement didn't come from a clever tuning parameter. It came from putting pgbouncer in front of the database, which cut the connection count from 200 to 20 without the application noticing.

This post covers what went wrong, what I changed, and what I'd do before running Postgres on any small server again.
